title: Atadwe Milkye
localName: Atadwe milkye — ataanme nmliche, atagbe mekye
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: Tiger nut pudding, one part rice to four parts tiger nuts — and do not boil it, it will thicken in a few minutes.
longDesc: A dairy-free pudding made from tiger nuts, which are not nuts but the tubers of a sedge, and which have been eaten since ancient Egypt. The ratio is the Ghanaian one: one part rice to four parts tiger nuts, so a cup of soaked chufa to a quarter cup of long grain rice. They are ground with a cup of water until powdery and as fine as you can get them, rinsed out with another half cup, squeezed through cheesecloth, rinsed again with two thirds of a cup and squeezed again. The milk is then heated over medium with a quarter cup of sugar, stirring constantly — and not boiled. It thickens in a few minutes and comes straight off the heat.
ingredients: 1/4 cup long grain white rice, or rice flour
1 1/2 cups plus 2/3 cup water — 1 cup to grind, 1/2 cup to rinse the processor, 2/3 cup to rinse the cheesecloth
A few drops of food colouring (optional)
equipment: Nonreactive bowls — plastic, glass, ceramic or stainless steel
steps: Remove any shrivelled or discoloured chufa — they may just float to the top — then rinse them well several times.

Put them into a nonreactive bowl to soak for several hours or overnight. In a cold kitchen with older nuts this means overnight in the refrigerator; in warm Ghana with fresh nuts it meant 3 or so hours.
Avoid leaving them to soak so long that they begin to ferment.
Drain, rinse once more and drain again.
Put the 1 cup of chufa and the 1/4 cup of rice into a food processor with 1 cup of water.
Grind and pulse several minutes until they are powdery and as fine as you can get them — somewhat like ground almonds. Push the mixture down with a spatula as needed.
Scrape the ground mixture into a nonreactive bowl. Add another 1/2 cup of water to the processor to rinse out as much of the dregs as possible, and mix it in with a spoon.
If you are using rice flour rather than whole rice, stir it in at this point.
Place a folded cheesecloth over a metal strainer set over another bowl. Scrape the mixture in, gather the edges and squeeze as much liquid as possible into the bowl.
Open the cheesecloth, pour in 2/3 cup of water, and squeeze again to force as much milk as possible through. Discard the dregs.
// Optional, as done in Ghana: strain the milk once more through a clean silk scarf for a finer result.
Pour the milk into a heavy nonreactive pan and add the salt and about 1/4 cup sugar.
Heat over medium, stirring constantly. DO NOT BOIL IT. It will thicken in a few minutes.
Immediately remove it from the heat and pour or ladle it into serving dishes.
Add a few drops of food colouring if you like, or layer several colours.
Allow to cool and serve topped with evaporated milk or cream.
chefTips: Do not boil it. That is the single instruction that matters and the author corrected herself on it between her draft and her tested version — it thickens in a few minutes over medium heat and comes straight off.
One to four, rice to tiger nuts, is the Ghanaian proportion. For a richer pudding, increase the rice.
The shrivelled and discoloured nuts float to the top when you rinse. That is the sorting cue and it saves picking through them.
Powdery and as fine as you can get them, somewhat like ground almonds. Under-grinding is the main cause of a thin, gritty pudding.
Nonreactive everything — bowls and pan. She repeats it three times, because tiger nut milk picks up metal.
Grinding the rice separately in a blender first is more elegant and makes no difference to the finished pudding. Her own verdict after making it both ways.
The silk scarf is how it is done in Ghana and it is optional. Her honest conclusion was that she could not reliably tell the difference.
Naturally off-white. Colouring it pink or yellow, or layering three colours, is a Ghanaian presentation and comes from Barbara Baeta.
commonMistakes: Boiling it, which splits and coarsens it.
Soaking so long the nuts begin to ferment.
Skipping the second water rinse through the cheesecloth, which leaves a third of the milk behind.
sources: Adapted from TWO POSTS by the same author, a draft and a tested version, published on consecutive days. The published recipe above follows the TESTED one.

PRIMARY: 'Recipe #26 (tested): Silky Tigernut Pudding (Atadwe Milkye)', betumiblog.blogspot.com. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 3:04 PM', timestamped 2009-11-05T15:04:00-05:00. Yield: NONE PRINTED. Quantities confirmed across two fetches, the second returning the complete formatted ingredient list and all eight numbered steps (TWO-PASS).

Ingredients exactly as printed: '1 cup of tigernuts (chufa)'; '1/4 cup of long grain white rice (or rice flour)'; '1/4 cup of sugar'; '1/4 - 1/2 teaspoon of salt (to taste)'; '1 1/2 cups plus 2/3 cups of water'; 'a few drops of food coloring (optional)'; 'milk or cream, for serving (optional)'. The plural 'cups' after 2/3 is a grammatical slip, not a quantity error — the water reconciles exactly with the method at 1 cup to grind, 1/2 cup to rinse the processor and 2/3 cup to rinse the cheesecloth.

THE OPERATIVE CUE, verbatim: 'Heat the milk over medium heat, stirring constantly. Do not boil it. It will thicken in a few minutes.' Followed by 'Immediately remove it from the heat'. NO NUMERIC COOK TIME is printed in the tested version — the endpoint is the thickening, not a clock.

THE GRINDING CUE, verbatim: 'Grind/pulse the nuts and rice several minutes until they are powdery and as fine as you can get them (somehow they reminded me of ground almonds).' THE SORTING CUE, verbatim: 'discard the shriveled or discolored ones, which may just float to the top'.

SECONDARY, AND IT CONTRADICTS THE PRIMARY: 'Recipe #26: Atadwe Milkye (Tiger Nut Pudding)', same blog, timestamped 2009-11-04T12:05:00-05:00, 'Posted by Fran at 12:05 PM'. This is a WORK IN PROGRESS written in the future tense, with no formatted ingredient list and the quantities embedded in prose, and it ends 'So, that's the basic recipe. I'll confirm it tomorrow.' It directs: 'bring it to a boil, then quickly reduce the heat to simmer, stirring constantly for about 10-12 minutes, until it thickens.' THE TESTED POST THE NEXT DAY SAYS 'Do not boil it' AND 'a few minutes'. THE DRAFT WAS NEVER AMENDED. Both readings are recorded; the tested, later, author-confirmed version is the one published, and the conflict is not averaged.

THE RATIO, from the draft and TWO-PASS: 'The proportions we used in Ghana were basically 1 to 4: one part rice to 4 parts tiger nuts.' And 'I was told for a richer version you can increase the rice.' Also, on local practice: 'Some people soak the nuts overnight, and some also soak the rice, but at Flair we did neither.'

ON FERMENTATION, and this is stated precisely rather than glossed: the source gives a fermentation BOUNDARY — 'Avoid leaving them to soak so long that they begin to ferment' — but NO OBSERVABLE SENSORY CUE for detecting the onset. What it supplies instead is ambient guidance: 'in November in cold Pennsylvania, with not-so-fresh chufa, this meant overnight in the refrigerator, but in warm Ghana with fresh nuts it meant 3 or so hours.' THE SOAK IS A HYDRATION SOAK, NOT A FERMENT — nothing in this recipe is deliberately fermented — so the collection's rule requiring a documented endpoint for fermented preparations does not bite here. The absence of a spoilage cue is recorded so that no entry implies one exists.

THE NAMES, quoted from the draft: 'apparently the Ga name for atadwe milkye is ataanme nmliche (thank you Anthia-Ofo). I believe the Ewe name is atagbe mekye (correct me if I'm wrong).' The author's own uncertainty is preserved.
AN UNRESOLVED NOTE the author herself flags: 'One cookbook from Ghana suggests coloring it with "black jack," which may be a mineral, but I'm not sure.' Recorded as printed, uncertainty included.

THE PRESENTATION, attributed on the page to Barbara Baeta of Flair Catering: 'Barbara says she likes to serve this in clear glass serving dishes, and sometimes colors it slightly yellow, or even layers it in 3 separate colors, like pink, yellow, and the natural color.'
THE REMARK WORTH KEEPING, verbatim: 'Who said the lactose-intolerant couldn't have pudding?' And on the silk scarf: 'it was like milking a cow to get all the liquid through the silk.'

ON SOURCING THE NUTS, recorded because it affects the soak: 'I was somewhat disappointed in the tiger nuts shipped from Valencia: in Ghana they were always very fresh, but these look like they've seen better days.'

ON TIGER NUTS: Cyperus esculentus, the tubers of a sedge rather than nuts, eaten in ancient Egypt and carried later to Spain, where the same tuber makes horchata de chufa. The author's observation is worth recording: 'even though all the online information about chufa acknowledges that the root/nut originated in ancient Egypt, and was carried later to Spain and Mexico, no one seems to realize that it's currently eaten in West Africa.'
NO YIELD is printed on either post. The four servings above is editorial.
storage: 3 days refrigerated, covered. It sets firmer as it chills.
healthBenefits: Tiger nuts are very high in resistant starch, a prebiotic fibre, plus magnesium and vitamin E.
Naturally dairy-free, so a pudding the lactose-intolerant can eat.
Vegan until the optional serving cream.
Lower in sugar than most set puddings.
culturalNote: Tiger nuts are sold in small heaps at Ghanaian markets and chewed raw as a snack; turning them into a pudding is the celebration version. That the same tuber makes Spanish horchata, and was eaten in pharaonic Egypt, makes atadwe milkye one of the oldest foods anyone still cooks.
